description:
¿Te imaginas convertir las visualizaciones de la Tierra de la NASA en música y hacer la ciencia terrestre más accesible a través del sonido?

Estamos creando un "Earth Jukebox": una interfaz que combina imágenes del Earth Information Center con sonificaciones generadas en tiempo real.
summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive 3D globe that turns NASA Earth observation data into sound, so people who are blind or have low vision can explore our planet's vital signs by listening.

We built a web app that shows near-real-time NASA data on a globe: air pollution (PM2.5 and five aerosol types from the GEOS-FP model), active fires (VIIRS) and rain and snow (GPM IMERG), all taken from NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations. Our backend turns NASA's published images back into real values. Users can click any point on Earth and hear what is happening there. Fixed rules map the data to sound: more pollution gives a deeper, denser drone; heavier rain gives more drops, wind and thunder; stronger fires give louder crackles and flames. A spoken description explains what is being heard.

The EIC's visualizations are compelling but almost entirely visual, which leaves out millions of people. Earth Jukebox makes this information accessible through sound, and it also offers sighted users a new, intuitive and emotional way to understand our changing planet.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Earth Jukebox is a web app that displays NASA Earth observation data on an interactive 3D globe and turns it into sound. Users select a data layer, rotate the globe, and click a location to explore conditions through sound.

Air quality: surface PM2.5 from the EIC daily visualization (GEOS-CF model), alongside five aerosol types from the near-real-time GEOS-FP model: dust, sea salt, sulfate, black carbon, and brown carbon.

Wildfires: fire radiative power from VIIRS active fire detections.

Precipitation: rain and snow rates from the GPM IMERG satellite precipitation product.

Our backend retrieves NASA’s published visualizations and reconstructs approximate physical values (µg/m³, MW, and mm/h) using NASA’s own color scales. Aerosol composition is retrieved directly as numerical data from GEOS-FP. The data is packaged into compact time-indexed grids covering recent hours or days, which the globe animates.

When a user selects a location, the browser reads the corresponding grid values and generates a 15-second sound clip using deterministic rules. PM2.5 controls the intensity of a low drone, wind, and dust-like textures. Rain becomes droplets, wind, and thunder. Fire becomes crackling that intensifies with fire radiative power. Spoken descriptions explain what users are hearing and whether levels are rising or falling.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The EIC’s visualizations are compelling, but their predominantly visual format creates barriers for people who are blind or have low vision. Earth Jukebox offers another way to explore this information through sound and spoken descriptions.

For sighted users, it also offers a more intuitive and emotional way to experience conditions across the planet. Our goal is to make NASA’s Earth science data more inclusive and demonstrate that sonification can be a meaningful tool for science communication, rather than a decorative effect.

Tools and Technologies

Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, and Pydantic for a typed, documented API; NumPy, Pillow, and OpenEXR for data processing and image decoding; uv for dependencies; pytest (reported 100% test coverage), ruff, and mypy for quality.

Frontend: plain JavaScript ES modules with no build step, MapLibre GL for the 3D globe, Three.js for the landing page, the Web Audio API for real-time sound synthesis, and HTML and CSS.

Infrastructure: Docker and Docker Compose, with nginx serving the website and proxying the API through a single origin.

NASA data: Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center visualizations, GEOS-FP via OPeNDAP, GIBS Blue Marble imagery, and NASA Black Marble night lights. No API keys are required.

Creativity

Rather than requiring new data products, we reconstruct approximate numerical values from NASA’s existing public visualizations. This connects the information users hear to the same visual sources they see, while acknowledging the limitations of image-based decoding.

Each phenomenon has its own soundscape—wind and thunder for storms, crackling for fire, and a low drone for polluted air—and its own visual treatment inspired by NASA’s visualizations, including glowing embers, rain clouds, and drifting haze. Each layer is recognizable through both sound and sight.

Factors We Considered

Accessibility: meaningful sound, spoken descriptions, and support for users who prefer reduced motion.

Scientific transparency: each source has a clearly defined role. Levels are described relative to NASA’s scales, not presented as official health indices. Values reconstructed from images are approximate.

Data validation: unknown precipitation colors stop the build. Some other changes, including changes to hard-coded color-scale endpoints, would require manual updates; see the limitations below.

Reliability: if NASA’s servers become unavailable, the app continues serving the latest successfully processed data.

Privacy: no accounts, user data collection, or tracking.

Simplicity and scalability: a clean, tested architecture with a clear path for growth.

Technical Documentation and Data Snapshot

Editorial note: Original figures are reproduced unchanged. Text embedded within these images remains in its original language; the surrounding document text and tables have been translated into English.

Earth Jukebox turns four NASA products into sound: PM2.5 particles, aerosol composition, active fires, and precipitation. The technical sections explain where the data comes from, how it is transformed, and what it shows on November 15, 2026.

All figures were calculated from the same files served by the production API. Each file was checked against the SHA-256 hash in its manifest. Global averages are area-weighted using the cosine of latitude so polar regions are not overrepresented.

We use four public NASA products, none requiring an API key. The data API connects to only two servers: svs.gsfc.nasa.gov and opendap.nccs.nasa.gov.

How We Process the Data

NASA publishes three of the four sources as images rather than numerical data. The backend reconstructs values using NASA’s own color bars, cleans them, and downsamples them to grids the browser can download.

Earth Jukebox data pipeline · 6 steps

Step 1 runs at most once every 15 minutes, and only when someone requests the scene. If NASA has not published anything new, nothing is downloaded.

For each time step and species, the browser receives between 16 and 64 times fewer values than the original image.

Common Scene Format

This is the contract between the backend and frontend, shared by all four sources:

•manifest.json: the grid, time axis, provenance, and, for each species, the unit, minimum, maximum, color scale, and SHA-256 hash.

•One .f32 file per species: little-endian float32 values ordered as [time step][latitude][longitude], from south to north and west to east. The version is included in the URL, so a published file never changes.

SVS 4285 uses discrete colors rather than a gradient. Each color represents a class, assigned the geometric midpoint of its range.

What the Data Shows (November 15, 2026)

Surface PM2.5

The global average is 2.02 µg/m³, and 84.8% of the planet is in the “very low” level on NASA’s scale. High values are concentrated in East and South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

The five levels divide NASA’s logarithmic scale into five equal intervals. These are the same labels used by the air sound and point information card; they are not an official air quality index.

Aerosol Composition

Sea salt accounts for 42% of global optical depth, followed by sulfate at 28%. Black carbon, which comes mainly from combustion, accounts for just 5%.

Changes Over Recent Hours

These are the time steps played through by the globe animation and 3D sound. Average PM2.5 fell from 2.24 to 1.83 µg/m³ before rising to 2.02. Rain consistently covered between 15.8% and 17.0% of the planet.

Active Fires

On the latest day with complete data (November 7), fire is present in 3,015 cells measuring 0.7° × 0.7°. Median fire radiative power is 1.35 MW and the maximum reaches 8 MW, the upper end of NASA’s color bar.

The 7 newest frames were discarded because NASA had not yet completed them. The decline over the final two days may partly reflect frames that are still incomplete: the filter only discards frames whose number of fire pixels is less than 0.6 times the median.

Precipitation

At each time step, rain covers 16–17% of the planet and snow covers 1.1–1.4%. Of the area receiving rain, 92.9% experiences light rain. Maximum values in the last time step are 34.6 mm/h for rain and 10.2 mm/h for snow.

From Data to Sound

Each sound depends on a single number between 0 and 1: its intensity, calculated from the value at the selected point. All sound parameters are formulas based on that number.

•Clip: 15 s (12 s of sound and 3 s of reverberation), stereo, 44.1 kHz.

•Stereo: values are also sampled in 32 directions around the point, and the sound is louder from the side with higher values. East is heard on the right.

•3D with headphones (rain and fire): each cell within a 300–400 km radius becomes a source at its actual direction and distance, using the acoustic responses of the KEMAR artificial head. North is heard in front and above. The clip plays through all scene time steps in 9 s.

Limitations

•PM2.5, fire, and precipitation values are read from NASA images, not from the underlying scientific products. Values are approximate; precipitation is represented by classes.

•Data age: GEOS-FP lags by about 12 h, PM2.5 updates once a day, the latest usable fire frame is several days old, and precipitation data is about 5 h old.

•The PM2.5 and fire scale endpoints are hard-coded. If NASA changed its legend, values would become inaccurate without triggering an error.

•This document is a snapshot from November 15, 2026. Scenes update automatically, so application figures change daily.
